questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose to study in Beijing because it was important to me to be in mainland China. I wanted to experience what it’s really like to live in China and to immerse myself in its culture and history.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, my experience was highly positive in terms of the academic quality of the program, the friendships I formed, and the meaningful personal and cultural memories I gained during my time there. However, the poor organization and the lack of clear responsibility between Bisu and KU created ongoing challenges. Communication issues between the two institutions often caused confusion around administrative matters, which led to unnecessary stress and sometimes took away from the overall experience

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: BISU did not provide much clarity or take clear responsibility. Information was often hard to find, and it was difficult to communicate with them when questions came up. When I did receive answers, they were sometimes inconsistent, which caused confusion and added stress.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Upon arrival at BISU a few days before registration day, we received several emails with important information. However, the emails were overwhelming and unnecessarily complicated, which caused stress given the limited amount of time we had to read through and follow all the rules and required documents.
After arriving at BISU, most information was shared through a WeChat group that included new students and teachers. This group became the main way to receive updates and ask questions. The first few days were very practical and focused on completing many administrative tasks, such as document submission, registration, student card collection, health checks, class division, and other requirements for new students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer:
There was little direct guidance from teachers, and students were generally expected to manage these processes independently. However, it was possible to ask questions in the group or contact teachers privately if needed.
There was very little assistance, along with a clear lack of responsibility and communication. It often felt as though the different teachers and staff members in charge were not communicating with each other. As a result, information was inconsistent, and students were frequently given unclear or conflicting instructions, which made the process more stressful and confusing than necessary

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
At first, we were living on campus, but the dormitories needed renovation, so we were required to move out. The university said they would provide alternative dorms, but there was a lot of confusion and unclear information, and it was hard to trust that the conditions would be acceptable. Because of this uncertainty, I decided to find my own accommodation and moved off campus about a month and a half later.
Living on campus also felt very restrictive, as there were many rules imposed by the dorm staff. About two months into the semester, it was officially announced that all students would have to move out of the dorms. The alternative housing that was offered was in very poor condition and located far from the university, not even on campus. For this reason, I was relieved that I had already found my own place.
Finding accommodation off campus was not extremely difficult, but since I was only staying for one semester, many landlords required a minimum one-year lease. I was very fortunate to find a small apartment only a ten-minute walk from campus, which made my living situation much more stable and comfortable.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Never trust the university when it comes to dorms. This semester, there were many problems, and the way the school handled them was even worse. They showed no responsibility, didn’t fix anything, and seemed to care very little about the students’ frustrations. It often felt like they were just going through the motions without actually helping. They would say not to worry, but then they offered very poor options at the last minute, leaving us to decide quickly whether to accept their choice or find our own place. If you can live on campus, I would definitely recommend it since it’s more convenient for everything. However, if there are problems with dorm availability or moving (like I experienced this semester), it’s better to find your own accommodation. Living off campus gives you more privacy, no strict rules, and you don’t have to deal with the uncertainty or other issues that can come with dorm life.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: When I lived in the dorms during the first 1.5 months, the room itself was quite nice and spacious, with a large closet, desk, and bed. The bathroom, however, was in somewhat poor condition. The kitchen was shared, and personal appliances like stoves or electric kettles were not allowed; staff would come to check the rooms. The best thing about dorm life was the convenience and, aside from the rules, the dorm community was quite fun and social.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: A bit confusing and complicating a lot of things to get done.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You had to go to different buildings on campus to complete the registration, which made a lot of walking and was a bit tiring, but the process itself was not very difficult.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can ask the teachers for help, if they don't know they usually are willing to guide you for further help

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: We were divided into classes based on the oral and online tests we completed, and I was very satisfied with the class I was placed in. If the level felt too difficult, students also had the option to switch classes.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don’t stress too much, even though there are times when strict deadlines can feel overwhelming. I noticed that many people didn’t complete everything on time, and it usually wasn’t a big issue. Going through the registration process with friends definitely helps, or finding people to complete it with, since it can be confusing—especially in a foreign country. Supporting each other makes the whole experience much easier.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I really liked that the classes were organized based on language level, as it suited me perfectly. Because of this, learning felt much easier and more effective compared to my course at UCPH. I just had to get used to the way they were teaching in China.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of the courses was well matched to my language abilities, which made the learning process both manageable and effective. Being placed in a class based on my actual level allowed the teaching to be more focused and structured, and I felt that the pace was appropriate without being overwhelming. This made it easier to follow the material, participate in class, and see clear progress in my language skills compared to my previous studies.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
You get divided in class based on your level. For me my level was bit higher than my other danish classmates. The language courses were divided into six different subjects, and I was placed in 中级三班, which was slightly more challenging than some of the other classes. I could clearly feel a difference compared to my classes in Denmark. In China, most lessons were teacher-led, with students listening, practicing, and completing exercises under the teacher’s guidance. In Denmark, the classes felt more focused on group work and independent student activities.
I personally preferred the course structure in China, as it felt more effective, more challenging, and, most importantly, faster-paced, which helped me make progress more quickly.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Intermediate Chinese, Intermediate Spoken Chinese, Intermediate Writing, Intermediate Reading, Intermediate Chinese Reading, Intermediate Listening, Intermediate Audiovisual Chinese by Video

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *

questions.answer: The language course

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The music club. The school organized New Year event performances that students could attend or take part in. In October and November, the school also held a cultural day for international students, which was very fun and interesting.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The cultural day was very fun and interesting to visit different booths from different countries

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: You can visit the city or if you wanna go to other city like Tianjin which was very close to Beijing I would recommend.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
Quite easy since im from a Chinese household, and I've been to china many times before.

But if your Chinese is very limited I would say it's quite hard to begin with because the teachers, staff and everything is in Chinese. Housing as well is very hard to to do when you don't speak Chinese.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I actually didn't interact with local students, most of the time was international.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not challenging but you just have to get used to the social norms in public etc.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The locals were very nice and helpful, which made adjusting to life in a new country much easier. Whether I needed directions, advice, or help with everyday tasks, people were generally friendly and willing to assist.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
To be aware of the lack of responsibility from both BISU and UCPH. I faced many problems related to my passport, and there was very little communication or coordination between the two schools when I needed help. I had expected KU to take a more active role when issues arose, but as an individual, I ended up having to handle most of the problems on my own. The UCPH coordinator was not very helpful, which caused a lot of stress. UCPH provided very little information beforehand, so when I arrived at BISU, I was surprised by many things that I hadn’t been informed about.

Get your Chinese apps and vpn ready, do research so you don't get too lost when you arrive.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Honestly, the best way to get accurate information is to contact students who have already studied abroad. Asking the coordinators, UCPH, or BISU often doesn’t provide the real answers or the detailed information you need. Try to gather as much information as possible before you go to avoid being overwhelmed and to reduce unnecessary stress.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The memories I made are unforgettable. I met so many amazing people whom I will cherish forever. Despite the poor organization between the schools and BISU, the friendships and experiences I gained made the entire experience truly worthwhile.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: There are a lot of practical things you have to take care of when you are in China. The country is quite strict about rules, and your passport is required for many processes. Almost everything is digital—transport cards, paying for meals, ordering food, and receiving packages—which makes life very convenient and easy. However, the process can be frustrating if something doesn’t work, and it’s often unclear who to ask for help. That’s why having friends in China is so important and helpful.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Enjoy it, this has been one of the best experiences of my life. There were many ups and downs, but for me personally, it was completely worth it. I met amazing people, made lifelong friendships, and learned so much—not just academically, but also about myself and the world. Living in China was incredible: it was convenient, full of delicious food, and had so many fun places to explore. The challenges I faced only made the experience more meaningful and helped me grow. Overall, studying in China was unforgettable and something I will always treasure.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
